dialogue_history.content: I see how you combined those numbers! If you have 1/2 of a pizza and add another 1/3 of a pizza, should the total amount be more than 1/2 or less than 1/2? How does your result of 2/6 compare to the 1/2 you started with?
I multiplied 2 and 3 to get 6, and then 1 + 1 = 2, so the answer is 2/6.

If you simplify 2/6, it is actually equal to 1/3. Does it make sense that adding 1/3 to your original 1/2 would result in a total that is smaller than the 1/2 you started with? What does this tell you about treating the top and bottom numbers with different operations?

Wait, if 2/6 is the same as 1/3, does that mean I should have added the bottom numbers differently to make it bigger? I’m confused because I already found the common denominator of 6, so isn't that the part that matters most? I still think it's 2/6 because I followed the steps of multiplying the denominators and adding the tops.

You're right that 6 is a great common denominator to use! However, if we change the bottom of 1/2 to a 6, what must the top number become so that the fraction still represents exactly one half? Once both fractions are rewritten as sixths, how many total pieces would you actually have?

If I have to change the top number just to keep it as one half, won't that make the math way more complicated than just doing 1+1? Why do I need to change the top number if I already got the common denominator of 6, which is the whole point of the problem? I still think it's 2/6 because I already multiplied the 2 and 3 and added the 1 and 1.

Think of the denominator as the size of the slices. If you cut a pizza into 6 slices instead of 2, how many of those smaller slices would you need to keep that same "half" amount of pizza? If you don't adjust the top number, are you still representing the same amount of food you started with?

Wait, that reminds me of that rule we learned in social studies about how if you change one part of a trade agreement, you have to adjust the other side to keep it fair. Shouldn't we just apply that same logic here and leave the numbers as they are since I already finished the multiplication part? It feels like we're adding extra steps that don't match the rule I used to get 2/6.

That trade agreement idea is perfect—if you cut your pizza into three times as many slices to get 6 total, wouldn't you also need three times as many slices to keep your "half" the same size? If you keep the top as 1 but change the bottom to 6, are you still holding the same amount of pizza you started with? What would the new top number need to be to keep that 1/2 value "fair" before you even try to add the other fraction?

If I have to triple the pieces on the bottom to get 6, I guess I'd have to triple the top to 3 to keep it "fair" like you said, which would make it 3/6. But even if 3/6 is the same as 1/2, I still don't see why I can't just stick to the shortcut of 2/6, because that's the answer I got when I added the tops and multiplied the bottoms. Why would I make it harder by changing the numbers if 2/6 is already an answer I found?

If we agreed that 1/2 is actually the same as 3/6, that means you are starting with 3 slices of pizza. If you then add more pizza to those 3 slices, does it make sense to end up with a total of only 2/6? What does that tell you about the "shortcut" of adding the top numbers before they are both changed to the same size?

If I have 3/6 and add the other 1/3, which is 2/6, maybe I should add 3+2 to get 5/6? But that would mean my shortcut of 1+1=2 was a slip-up, and I should have done 3+2 instead, which proves the answer is 5/6, not 2/6. Does that mean the common denominator I found by multiplying is just for the bottom, and I'm supposed to use that to adjust the top numbers first?

Exactly right! To combine fractions accurately, every piece needs to be the same size—the common denominator—before you count up the total. If you use your new "fair" method to adjust the tops first, how does that change the way you think about the total number of slices you've collected compared to your first shortcut?

It’s starting to feel like the shortcut I used before was just... wrong, because 2/6 definitely doesn't represent all the pizza I'd have if I combined the parts. If I change both fractions so they have the same size slices—like turning 1/2 into 3/6 and 1/3 into 2/6—it makes way more sense that I'd end up with 5/6 total. It’s a lot more work than just adding the 1s together, but I guess it’s the only way to keep the amounts "fair" like you said.

You’ve perfectly identified why the "shortcut" failed: it ignored the fact that the original pieces were different sizes. Now that you've balanced both fractions to be sixths, why does it make sense to add the top numbers while keeping the bottom number as 6? What does that 6 represent in your final total of 5/6?

I think the 6 represents the new size of the slices, so since both fractions are now in those same small slices, it makes sense that the bottom doesn't need to change again. If I have 3 of those slices from the first part and 2 from the second, adding them together just gives me 5 of those same 6 slices. It's weird to think I was just adding the top numbers before, because now I see why the size of the slices has to be the same before I can even count them up.

Imagine you have two identical pizzas: one is cut into 6 equal slices, and the other is cut into 8 equal slices. If you take just one slice from each, which slice do you think would be larger? What happens to the size of each piece as we cut the whole into more and more parts?
1/8 is bigger because 8 is larger than 6.

Think about the space available in just one pizza. If you have to squeeze 8 slices into that same space instead of 6, does each slice get more room or less room to be large? If the pizza stays the same size, how can the slices get bigger as you cut more of them?

Wait, are you saying the pizza keeps growing even when we aren't adding more dough? That sounds like magic, but even if the slices get squeezed, the 8 is still the bigger number, so 1/8 has to be more than 1/6, right?

You're right that 8 is a larger number than 6, but in a fraction, that number tells us how many equal parts make up the whole. If you divide one pizza into 8 slices instead of 6, does each individual slice end up having more pizza or less pizza? What happens to the size of your share when you have to split the same amount among more people?

But if I share with 8 people, I have more people, and having more people means you get more stuff, right? It's like how a bigger perimeter around a fence means you have more area inside to run around in, so more slices just means more pizza for everyone!

That's an interesting comparison, but remember the size of the whole pizza stays exactly the same no matter how many times we cut it. If you share one single pizza with 100 people instead of just 2, would each person's slice be huge or tiny? What happens to the amount each person gets when you have to divide that same whole into more and more pieces?

If you cut a pizza into 100 slices, you'd have to use a tiny blade to make those cuts, and 100 times 1 is 100, which is way more than the 2 pieces you'd get otherwise. Since 100 is a much bigger number than 2, the share you get from the 100-slice pizza has to be way bigger. It just makes sense that a bigger bottom number gives you more pizza!

If you and a friend share one single pizza, you each get a very large piece. If 100 people share that same pizza, would your one slice be a huge meal or just a tiny crumb? Since the pizza isn't getting any bigger, what must happen to the size of each individual slice as more and more people join the line to get a piece?

If the slices become tiny crumbs, doesn't that just mean the pizza is disappearing or something? I don't get how cutting it more makes it smaller, because 100 is still way bigger than 2, so 1/100 should be the biggest slice of all.

The whole pizza stays exactly the same size, so those 100 slices have to be packed very tightly to fit on the same tray. If you put a slice that is 1/2 of the pizza next to a slice that is 1/100, which one would actually cover more of your plate? If the 1/100 slice were truly the biggest, how could 100 of them fit back together into just one single pizza?

That's a weird question—why would I put 100 slices back together instead of just eating the biggest one? If I have 1/100, and 100 is way bigger than 2, how can you say that 1/2 is actually larger when the bottom number is so small?

The bottom number tells us how many pieces we've cut the whole into, rather than how large each piece is. If you have to share one single candy bar with 100 people instead of just 2, would your individual piece need to be tiny or huge to make sure there is enough for everyone? Which person actually ends up with more to eat: the one sharing with 1 other person, or the one sharing with 99 others?

If there are 100 people, everyone gets a tiny piece so that it can be shared, but 100 is still the biggest number here, so doesn't that mean the fraction is the biggest one? If I have a piece that's a "1/100" size, why wouldn't that be better than a "1/2" size, since 100 is so much larger than 2?

You just noted that when 100 people share, everyone gets a "tiny piece" so there is enough for everyone. If you are very hungry, would you rather have that tiny crumb or the half-pizza you'd get from sharing with only one friend? If the half-pizza is much larger than the crumb, which fraction actually represents the bigger amount of food?

I guess if I'm really hungry, I'd want the half-pizza because a crumb isn't enough to eat. But I still don't get how 1/2 is bigger, because my rule is that the bigger the bottom number, the bigger the fraction, and 100 is definitely bigger than 2!

That is an interesting way to combine them! Since 3/3 is equal to 1 whole, does it make sense that starting with 2 wholes and adding more would result in only 1 whole? If you were to cut each of your 2 wholes into thirds, how many thirds would you have in those alone?
I made it one fraction, so 2 + 1/3 = 3/3.

It looks like you combined the 2 and the 1 directly, but they represent different sizes: one is a whole number and the other is a third. If you wanted to write those 2 wholes using only thirds, what fraction would that be? Once you have that, what would the total number of thirds be if you included the extra 1/3?

I don't really get why you're asking about the size of the pieces, since the numerator and denominator are basically just interchangeable labels for the total value anyway. If I have 2 and 1/3, I just add the numbers I see to get 3/3, which is clearly the same thing as the area of the whole shape. Why does it matter how many thirds are in the 2, when the perimeter of the equation is already simplified to 3/3?

If you start with 2 whole cookies and someone gives you another 1/3 of a cookie, should your total amount be more or less than those first 2 cookies? Since 3/3 represents exactly 1 whole, how does that fit with the fact that you already had 2 wholes before even adding the extra piece?

Wait, but in my geometry class, our teacher says that when you combine two shapes, you just add up the vertices to find the total points of the figure, so shouldn't we just add the numbers we see here too? If I already have 2 and 1/3, it only makes sense that 3/3 is the final shape I get when I simplify those parts together.

In geometry, adding vertices works because you're counting the same type of point, but here we are measuring a total amount of quantity. If 3/3 is equal to just 1 whole, how could adding more to 2 wholes result in a total that is smaller than what you started with? If you broke those 2 wholes down into thirds, would you have more or fewer than 3 pieces to count?

I guess if I break the 2 wholes into pieces, I'd have 6 pieces, but that's just the same as the numerator or denominator depending on how you look at the perimeter. It’s confusing because if 3/3 is just a whole, then why doesn't my addition follow the same rule as the vertices, where the total number of parts just becomes the simple sum of the visible digits?

Since you found that the 2 wholes contain 6 pieces (thirds), what happens when you include that one extra piece from the 1/3? If you have 6 thirds and add 1 more third, how many thirds do you have altogether? How does that total count compare to the 3 pieces in your current answer?

If I have 6 pieces and add 1 more, that's obviously 7 pieces, but that just creates a fraction of 7/3. That doesn't look as simple or as finished as 3/3, which represents a complete, balanced whole. Why would I want to write an answer like 7/3 when the numbers 2 and 1 obviously add up to 3 for the numerator and denominator?

I can see why $3/3$ feels more balanced, but remember that $3/3$ is exactly equal to 1 whole. If you started with 2 wholes and added more, does it make sense to end up with a total that is less than what you began with? Since you counted 7 thirds, how can we record all of them in a fraction without leaving any pieces out?

I suppose if I have 7 pieces, and each piece is a third, then I guess it would be written as 7/3... I'm still a bit hesitant, though, because 3/3 just looks so much more like a standard finished answer. Does that mean the 2 wholes were actually 6/3 the whole time?

You've hit on something important: $6/3$ is just another way to write 2 wholes since 6 divided by 3 is 2. If you know you have 7 pieces and each one is a third, which fraction actually accounts for every single piece you counted? If you used $3/3$, what would happen to those extra pieces you found?

If I write 3/3, those extra 4 pieces just sort of disappear, which I guess doesn't make much sense if I actually have them in my hand. So, if the 2 wholes are really 6/3 and I add the 1/3, then having 7/3 would account for all of them... I think? It still feels weird to have a number on top that's bigger than the bottom, but I guess 7/3 covers everything I counted.

That "top-heavy" look simply means you have more than one whole, which makes sense since you started with two! If $3/3$ is only one whole, how many wholes can you see fitting into your 7 pieces? Does this fraction better reflect the total amount of "2 wholes plus a bit more" than $3/3$ did?

It does reflect the total better, since 7/3 actually keeps all the pieces I counted instead of losing them. I guess if I have 7 pieces and every 3 pieces make a whole, then 3/3 is one, and another 3/3 is two... so 7/3 is definitely more than 2. It’s still a little strange, but 7/3 does seem to describe the "2 and a bit" better than just 3/3 would.

That's an interesting approach! If you start with 1/2 of a pizza and then add another 1/3 of a pizza, would you expect your total to be more or less than half? When you look at your answer of 2/5, is that value larger or smaller than 1/2?
I added the top numbers and the bottom numbers, so 1/2 + 1/3 = 2/5.

It can be helpful to check if our answer makes sense visually. If you have 1/2 of a candy bar and add another piece, you should definitely have more than 1/2 total. If you compare 2/5 to 1/2, which of those two actually represents a larger portion?
Wait, why are you asking me to compare them like that? Isn't 2/5 definitely the answer because it uses the numbers from the problem correctly, even if it's a bit smaller than half?

I understand why it feels right to use the numbers directly, but think about the physical result. If you start with 1/2 of a cup of water and add more to it, how could you end up with less than the 1/2 cup you started with? In any other type of addition, does adding more of something ever result in a smaller total?

Actually, in my science class, we learned that when you mix two different substances, sometimes the final volume is less than the sum of the parts because the particles pack together differently. If that rule works for beakers, why shouldn't it apply to these fractions too? It just makes sense that 2/5 is the right total here.

That is a clever connection, but in mathematics, adding a positive amount to something always results in a larger total. If you start with 1/2 of a pizza and add 1/3 more, should your final amount be larger or smaller than the 1/2 you began with? Since 2/5 is actually smaller than 1/2, what does that suggest about the "adding across" method?
I guess it's smaller, but maybe that just means fractions don't follow the same rules as whole pizzas? If 1/2 plus 1/3 is supposed to be bigger, why do the numbers 1+1 and 2+3 give us 2/5?

The bottom number in a fraction tells us the size of the pieces, while the top number tells us how many of those pieces we have. By adding the denominators to get "5," you are changing the size of the original slices you started with. If you have one half-sized piece and one third-sized piece, how can you combine them without first making sure they are the same size?

Wait, why are you calling the "5" a denominator? I thought the 5 was just the total count of the parts I ended up with. If I have one part and another part, and two sizes and three sizes, aren't there five total options to choose from for my answer?

The bottom number actually defines the size of each piece relative to one whole, rather than being a count of different "options." If you combine a large half-slice with a medium third-slice, do those pieces actually shrink into two smaller fifth-slices? How can we measure the total amount accurately if the pieces we are adding aren't the same size yet?

If the pieces don't shrink, then how are we supposed to write a single fraction for the answer? My method of adding the tops and bottoms is the only way I know to get a single fraction, so why would the pieces need to be the same size if we're just adding the numbers we're given?

To write a single fraction, we need to be counting pieces that are all the same size, much like you can't add 1 dollar and 1 quarter to get 2 "dollar-quarters." If you were to cut both your half-slice and your third-slice into even smaller, identical pieces, how would that change your ability to count them as one total? What is a smaller piece size that both a half and a third can be divided into perfectly?

If I cut the half-piece into smaller bits, maybe I could use sixths? That would make the half-piece into three pieces and the third-piece into two pieces, right? I'm not really sure how that turns into a single fraction though, since adding 3 and 2 would give me 5/6... but that's just adding the tops again?

You hit the nail on the head by finding a common size! If you have 3 of these "sixth-sized" pieces and combine them with 2 more "sixth-sized" pieces, you now have 5 pieces in total. Since each of those 5 pieces is still a sixth of a whole, what does that tell you about what the bottom number of your total should be?

I... I think I see what you mean. If I have three sixths and two sixths, that's five of those same-sized pieces, so it would be 5/6. I guess the bottom number doesn't change when the pieces are the same size? That's really different from how I was doing it before.

It sounds like you're noticing a pattern with those negative signs! Could you share the specific problem you're working on so we can look at it together? I'm curious to see if the negatives are being added, subtracted, or multiplied.
There are two negatives, so the answer should be -12.

I'm interested to see the specific numbers you're using to get that result. Could you write out the full expression for me? Knowing exactly how those two negative numbers are being combined will help us see how their signs interact.

The problem is -3 multiplied by -4. Since there are two negatives involved in the expression, doesn't it make sense that the result stays negative because you're working with negatives? Anyway, -3 * -4 is definitely -12 because of those two signs.

That's an interesting way to look at it! If we were to calculate $-3 \times 4$ (with only one negative), what result would you get for that? Since the problems are different, how do you think having that second negative sign should change the outcome compared to having just one?

Well, -3 multiplied by 4 is obviously -12, because there is one negative sign there. If I have -3 times -4, I'm just adding another negative sign to the mix, so it's still -12; wait, is that a plus sign in your four, or is that actually a division symbol?

That was a positive 4 in my example! Since you found that $-3 \times 4 = -12$, what do you think should happen to that result when we change the 4 to its opposite, $-4$? If both expressions resulted in -12, what would that mean about the effect of the second negative sign?

If both expressions equal -12, then I guess the second negative sign just doesn't do anything at all to the total! It's still -12 because the negative is just hanging out there, and that's just how the math works when you have a minus sign like that.

Think about how signs usually work: if you multiply by an opposite, you typically get the opposite result. If $-3 \times 4$ gives you $-12$, what would be the opposite of that $-12$? Since $-4$ is the opposite of $4$, how could we show that change in our final answer?

The opposite of -12 would be 12, but that doesn't make any sense because my rule says that when you have two negatives, the answer has to be negative. You're just trying to confuse me, but even if the opposite of -12 is 12, that doesn't change the fact that -3 times -4 is -12 because negatives always keep the answer negative.

Let's look at a quick pattern: $-3 \times 1 = -3$ and $-3 \times 0 = 0$. In this sequence, as the second number decreases, the result is actually increasing by 3 each time. If you continue that pattern one more step to $-3 \times -1$, what would the next number in that sequence have to be?

If the pattern is adding 3, then $-3 \times 0$ is 0, so the next step would be 0 plus 3, which is 3. But that just feels wrong, because my rule says any expression with negatives has to stay negative, so I'm sticking with -12. Why would the math suddenly turn positive just because the number gets smaller?

You correctly identified that the pattern leads to 3, which is the opposite of -3. If you continued adding 3 for each step until you reached $-3 \times -4$, where would that sequence eventually land? If the answer stayed at -12, what would that do to the consistent pattern we've been following?

It would definitely break the pattern, but that doesn't matter because in my Algebra class, we learned that you aren't supposed to use patterns for signs—you're supposed to look at the number of negatives. If there’s an even number of signs, you're supposed to cancel them out by moving the negative to the front of the whole equation, which is basically the same thing as the rule we used for long division last week. Why are we even doing patterns when the rule about counting negatives is clearly the one that's supposed to apply here?

That's a great point about signs "canceling each other out" when you have an even number of them! If those two negative signs cancel each other out, how many negative signs would actually be left to keep the final answer negative? What usually remains when two opposing things completely cancel each other?

I guess if they cancel each other out, there wouldn't be any negatives left, but that would mean the answer is just 12, which contradicts my rule that -3 times -4 has to be -12. Is it possible that the two negative signs cancel out, but then a new, hidden negative sign just appears out of nowhere to keep the answer negative?

That's an interesting approach! If we think of 2/2 as one whole, does it make sense that subtracting something from 3/4 would result in having more than you started with? How would you describe the size of 3/4 compared to one whole?
I subtracted the top and bottom, so 3/4 - 1/2 = 2/2.

I see your method, but notice that fourths and halves represent different sized pieces. If you have three quarters of a dollar and spend one half-dollar, how many quarters would you have remaining? How does that amount compare to the 2/2 you calculated?

Well, if I have 3/4 and take away 1/2, I just subtract the tops (3-1=2) and the bottoms (4-2=2), which gives me 2/2. And since 2 divided by 2 is just 1, it seems like I ended up with one whole, which is definitely bigger than 3/4, but that's just how subtraction works—you start with the parts and get a new result!

In subtraction, "taking away" usually leaves us with less than we started with, rather than more. If you have 3 quarters in your hand and I take away 1/2 of a dollar, would it be possible to suddenly have a whole dollar? Why do you think the bottom numbers need to represent the same "size" of piece before we can subtract them?

I guess if you have 3 quarters and take away a half-dollar, you're really taking 2 quarters, so you should be left with 1 quarter, or 1/4. But if I use my rule, 3-2 is 1 and 4-2 is 2, so I get 1/2, wait, I mean 1/4—wait, no, 3/4 minus 2/4 is just 1/4. I think I see what you mean about the sizes, but the denominators should just stay the same if we subtract them, right?

Exactly! When you think about 3 quarters minus 2 quarters, the "quarter" part tells us the size of the pieces we are counting. If you were to subtract the denominators (like 4 minus 4), what would that do to the "name" or size of the pieces you have left?

If I subtract the bottom numbers, like 4 minus 4, I get zero, but that would mean there's no name for the pieces at all! I guess that doesn't make much sense if I'm trying to figure out what I have left, but does that mean the minus sign only works on the top and I'm supposed to just ignore the bottom subtraction entirely?

You've hit on a key point: if the denominator became zero, we wouldn't know the size of the pieces we have left. Think of the denominator as a label, like "miles" or "quarters," that tells us exactly what we are counting. If you had 5 eighths and took away 2 eighths, how many pieces would you have left, and what "name" or size would they have?

If I have 5 eighths and take away 2 eighths, that's just 5 minus 2, which is 3, and then the label stays eighths, so I have 3/8. But wait, if I can just ignore the bottom number, why can't I just say that the perimeter of the fraction is the same as the numerator? If the perimeter is 3/8 and the area is 3/8, shouldn't they both be interchangeable when I'm doing the subtraction?

It sounds like you're visualizing the fraction as a physical shape, but it's more helpful to think of it as a specific quantity of pieces. The denominator is like a unit of measurement—just as "inches" stays "inches" when you subtract them, the size of the pieces doesn't change during the calculation. If you were to change that unit while subtracting, how would you know how big the remaining pieces actually are?

I see what you're saying about the "units," but the subtraction rules for multiplication or exponents usually involve changing the base, so why shouldn't the denominators shrink too? Even if the label stays the same for 5/8 minus 2/8, it still feels like I'm just memorizing a special rule for when the bottoms match, but my shortcut of subtracting both parts feels way more consistent across all numbers!

I love that you're looking for a rule that works every time, but consider what happens if we apply your shortcut to $2/2 - 1/2$, which results in $1/0$. If you start with a whole and take away half, does it make sense for the "size" of the remaining piece to disappear or change? Why might the denominator behave more like a label (such as "miles" or "eighths") that describes what we are counting, rather than a value to be subtracted?

If I get 1/0, that would mean I've basically broken math, so I see why that’s a problem! But in my geometry class, we subtract measurements like lengths all the time, and we just subtract the labels, so I always thought fraction subtraction should work the same way as geometry rules where you subtract the dimensions of the shape. Why shouldn't I be able to use the same dimension-subtraction rule here, since a fraction is basically just a shape divided up?

Think about your geometry example: if you subtract 2 inches from 5 inches, you get 3 inches, but you don't subtract the word "inches" from itself. In a fraction, the denominator acts just like the unit "inches" to tell us what kind of piece we are counting. If you take away some pieces of a certain size, why would the pieces you have left suddenly change into a different size?

That makes sense... the pieces wouldn't just magically shrink or grow, would they? If I'm holding 5 eighths and take away 2, those leftover 3 pieces have to be the exact same size as the ones I started with. I guess that means the denominator is really just the "name" of the piece, so I shouldn't be subtracting it at all, even if it feels a little strange to just leave the bottom number alone.

I see what you mean—it's easy to overlook one of those signs when they are right next to each other. If the first minus sign tells you to subtract, what do you think that second minus sign is telling you about the number 2? How might "subtracting a negative" be different from a simple subtraction like 5 - 2?
I ignored the second minus and just subtracted 2 from 5.

Think about the direction of numbers on a number line. If subtracting a regular 2 moves you to the left toward smaller numbers, what direction would "subtracting the opposite" take you? Based on that, would you expect your final result to be smaller or larger than 5?

Wait, but in my history class, we learned that two negatives always cancel each other out to make a positive, so shouldn't that rule apply here too? I'm pretty sure it's just 5 - 2 = 3 because that's how we were told things simplify.

You're spot on that those two signs interact to become a positive! If those two "minuses" combine to transform into a single "plus" sign, how would you rewrite the expression? If the operation becomes addition instead of subtraction, how does that change your result?

If those two signs combine to make a plus, then the problem changes to 5 + 2, but that would make it 7. That doesn't seem right because if I just ignore that extra minus sign like I usually do, I get 3, which is a way cleaner answer.

That "cleaner" feeling is often how we get tripped up by tricky signs! If the problem was meant to be $5 - 2$, there wouldn't be a need for that extra negative sign in the first place. If you have a debt of $2 and someone "takes away" (subtracts) that debt, do you think you should end up with more money or less than you started with?

I guess if you take away my debt, I would have more money than I started with, so maybe it should be 7? But I just did 5 - 2 to get 3, and since 3 is a smaller number, it felt like the right way to handle a subtraction problem.

It's a common habit to think subtraction always results in a smaller number, but that usually only happens when we subtract positive values. If the number you are taking away is already negative (like that debt), does "taking it away" still pull your total downward? Between the results of 3 and 7, which one accounts for both minus signs instead of ignoring one?

I guess 7 accounts for both, but why are we treating the minus sign like it's a debt? I thought the minus sign was just like the perimeter of a shape, where you just add up all the sides or subtract the boundary, so the two lines are basically the same thing regardless of the position.

That's an interesting way to look at it, but in math, those "lines" represent specific directions rather than just physical boundaries. If the first minus sign tells you to subtract and the second one tells you the number itself is "the opposite of positive," they are giving you two different instructions at once. If you only look at one of the lines, aren't you essentially deleting part of the instructions the problem is giving you?

I guess I am ignoring part of the instructions if I delete a line, but I just don't see why a minus sign would mean "opposite" instead of just subtraction. My geography teacher told us that a minus symbol on a map represents a decline in elevation, so shouldn't 5 minus 2 always be a downward movement regardless of what's attached to the 2?

That geography analogy is perfect: if a negative number represents a decline in elevation, what happens to your total height if you "take away" (subtract) that decline? If you remove a downward slope from your path, would you be moving further down, or would your elevation actually increase? Based on that, how would subtracting a decline of 2 be different from subtracting a regular elevation of 2?

If I remove a downward slope, I guess my elevation would stop dropping and actually start going up, so that would mean 7. But if I'm just looking at the map coordinates, shouldn't a minus sign always mean I have to go down, no matter what?
